compoundNote: Tart cherry here means Montmorency tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) as juice, concentrate or powder. The sleep literature is dominated by juice and concentrate (typically 30 mL concentrate or 240 mL juice, once or twice a day); the product form on the Performance Lab Sleep label is CherryPURE, a branded powdered whole Montmorency tart cherry, stated as 500 mg at a 50:1 concentrated ratio per 2-capsule serving (the ratio and its basis are label claims we could not verify). PubMed shows CherryPURE only in two exercise trials at 480 mg/day, with no sleep outcome. Cherry-industry bodies fund much of this work (CherryPharm, Cherry Marketing Institute); funding is recorded per study. Melatonin in cherry juice is trace-level (about 0.135 micrograms in a juice dose in one analysis), so any sleep effect is not established to run through dietary melatonin. Evidence for sleep is small, short, mixed and mostly in juice; two trials that tested capsule or powder forms were null. No pooled meta-analysis exists. All pubmedUrl status values are 203 because NCBI served a bot-challenge page to curl; see statusNote.

verdicts.claim: Sleep duration/quality/efficiency, healthy adults (juice or concentrate)
verdicts.reason: Two small positive trials with juice or concentrate (Howatson 2012, n=20, 7 days, actigraphy: time in bed, total sleep time, efficiency up; Chung 2022, n=19 athletes, 48 h: time in bed, WASO and movement index improved) against two null trials in healthy adults (PMID 35790450, n=44, 30 days, juice and capsule arms; PMID 35564709, n=45, 20 days, concentrate, sleep a secondary measure). Samples are tiny, follow-ups are 1 to 4 weeks, and the positive Howatson paper is paywalled so its dose and funding could not be read. No pooled estimate exists.

verdicts.claim: Sleep in older adults with insomnia (juice)
verdicts.reason: Two crossover pilots, 15 and 8 completers. Pigeon 2010 (CherryPharm blend, 240 mL twice daily, 2 weeks): insomnia severity and wake after sleep onset improved vs placebo, but sleep latency, total sleep time and efficiency did not; the maker funded it entirely. Losso 2018 (240 mL twice daily, 2 weeks): polysomnographic total sleep time +84 min but latency, WASO and PSG efficiency unchanged and most questionnaires null; Cherry Marketing Institute funded it. Neither finding has been independently replicated, and the first is sponsor-funded, so this is hypothesis-generating only.

verdicts.claim: Sleep in clinical populations with other conditions (poor sleep with overweight or obesity)
verdicts.reason: One industry-funded crossover (n=34, 500 mg Montmorency powder 1 h before bed, 14 days) found no effect on any sleep or inflammation measure. Graded preliminary because it is a single null trial, not because there is positive evidence. Treat as no benefit shown.

verdicts.claim: Sleep from powdered/capsule tart cherry (the form used in Performance Lab Sleep)
verdicts.reason: No trial of a cherry powder or capsule used alone showed a sleep benefit. The two trials that included a capsule or powder arm were null (PMID 39683518: 500 mg, n=34; PMID 35790450: capsule arm within a n=44 trial). All positive single-ingredient sleep trials used juice or concentrate. The equivalence of powder to juice for sleep is not established (the 500 mg trial authors argue it matches 2 oz of concentrate by anthocyanin and polyphenol content, an assertion by the authors, not a tested bioequivalence).

verdicts.claim: Melatonin (urinary 6-sulfatoxymelatonin or plasma) increase from tart cherry
verdicts.reason: Higher urinary 6-SMT after juice concentrate (Howatson 2012) and after a cherry-extract product (Simper 2019, 28.95 vs 4.0 ng/ml) but that product contained no detectable melatonin; no change in plasma melatonin in the hockey trial. The Losso full text puts the melatonin in a juice dose at about 0.135 micrograms versus the 0.5-5 mg doses used for sleep, so food melatonin is unlikely to explain any sleep effect. A raised urinary metabolite is not itself a sleep outcome.

verdicts.claim: Sleep from multi-ingredient blends that include tart cherry plus tryptophan/magnesium
verdicts.reason: One 3-day crossover (n=16) of a tryptophan, glycine, magnesium, tart cherry powder and theanine blend improved latency (-24 min), sleep time (+22 min) and efficiency, whereas a 2-day replicate crossover (n=12 youth footballers) of a larger blend (cherry concentrate 15 g, tryptophan 200 mg, magnesium 300 mg, glycine 3 g and others) found trivial effects, and the cherry-extract product Night Time Recharge improved only sleep latency in 20 adults. None isolates cherry, none matches the Performance Lab Sleep formula, and exposures were 2 to 7 days.

verdicts.claim: Pooled evidence (meta-analysis) for tart cherry on sleep
verdicts.reason: No meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes was located. The only tart-cherry-specific review is a 2025 qualitative systematic review of 7 studies (3 with improved sleep indicators), which calls the evidence limited and heterogeneous.

doseAssessment.trialRange: Positive sleep results in humans used JUICE or CONCENTRATE, not powder: Pigeon 2010 two 8 oz (about 240 mL) servings/day for 14 days (older adults with insomnia; PSG-free diary data); Losso 2018 240 mL twice daily for 14 days (older adults; juice from 100 g cherries per dose, melatonin about 0.135 micrograms); Howatson 2012 concentrate for 7 days (amount in the paywalled paper; a secondary source says 30 mL twice daily, not verified); Chung 2022 30 mL concentrate diluted to 200 mL, 5 servings in 48 h. Null or negative trials: 500 mg/day Montmorency powder capsules for 14 days (PMID 39683518); capsules and 2 x 240 mL juice for 30 days (PMID 35790450); 30 mL concentrate twice daily for 20 days (PMID 35564709). CherryPURE (the brand on the Performance Lab label) appears in PubMed only in two exercise trials at 480 mg/day, with no sleep outcome.
doseAssessment.suggestedText: Performance Lab Sleep lists 500 mg of CherryPURE whole Montmorency tart cherry (50:1 concentrated ratio) per 2-capsule serving. That is the same milligram amount (500 mg of whole Montmorency powder, two capsules before bed) that produced NO sleep benefit in an industry-funded 14-day crossover of 34 adults with poor sleep and overweight or obesity (PMID 39683518), and it is a powder rather than the juice or concentrate that all the positive sleep trials used. Whether a '50:1' concentrate powder is equivalent to the unconcentrated powder in that trial, or to 2 oz of juice concentrate, is NOT established: the 50:1 ratio is a label claim we could not verify, we found no published analysis of CherryPURE, and the trial authors' statement that 500 mg powder matches 2 oz concentrate by anthocyanin and polyphenol content is their own claim. So the label dose is inside the range tested for powder (and that range was null), but its relationship to the juice doses that worked cannot be stated; do not convert 500 mg to millilitres of juice on the page.

safetySignals.signal: Juice and concentrate formats carry sugar and energy: a 30 mL concentrate dose is about 102 kcal per the manufacturer (the 20-day trial used 60 mL/day). Not relevant to a capsule, but relevant when comparing with the juice trials.
safetySignals.title: Effects of Montmorency Tart Cherry and Blueberry Juice on Cardiometabolic and Other Health-Related Outcomes: A Three-Arm Placebo Randomized Controlled Trial

safetySignals.signal: Losso 2018 screened for obstructive sleep apnoea by polysomnography: 3 of 11 randomised participants with insomnia had sleep apnoea and were excluded and referred, so the 'insomnia' group in cherry-juice trials may include untreated sleep disorders.
safetySignals.title: Pilot Study of the Tart Cherry Juice for the Treatment of Insomnia and Investigation of Mechanisms

gaps: No randomised sleep trial of a CherryPURE-labelled product was found: a PubMed search for 'CherryPURE' returned only two exercise trials (PMID 26578852, PMID 27231439) at 480 mg/day, neither with a sleep or melatonin outcome.

Every positive single-ingredient sleep result used juice or concentrate (Pigeon 2010, Losso 2018, Howatson 2012, Chung 2022). The two trials that included a capsule or powder arm were null (PMID 39683518, PMID 35790450). No head-to-head juice vs powder sleep comparison and no pharmacokinetic bridge between a '50:1' powder and juice was found.

Both older-adult insomnia trials are tiny crossover pilots (15 and 8 completers), 2 weeks each, and both were funded by cherry industry bodies (CherryPharm in full, Cherry Marketing Institute). The 2024 null trial was also Cherry Marketing Institute funded. No independent large RCT exists. A trial protocol exists (CherryZZZ, PMID 41901097: 16 oz juice/day vs placebo for 4 weeks, 20 older adults with insomnia) but no results had been published at search time.

Howatson 2012 (PMID 22038497), the main healthy-adult positive trial, is paywalled: the dose, participant ages, melatonin assay values and funding could not be read. The dose given in the notes comes from a 2025 secondary review that is internally inconsistent and was not checked against the primary paper.

Functional content of the juice 'melatonin' is minuscule (Losso: about 0.135 micrograms per dose), and the 6-SMT rise in a product with undetectable melatonin (PMID 31512550) means the melatonin mechanism is unproven. The suggested alternative mechanism (procyanidin B-2, IDO, tryptophan availability) comes from 8 completers plus Caco-2 cell work, not from replicated human data.

Doses for the blend trials (PMID 36094342, tryptophan/glycine/magnesium/tart cherry/theanine) are not in the abstract and the paper is paywalled; the funding is unverified. The magnesium and tryptophan doses in the Performance Lab formula (100 mg and 200 mg) are not tested here.

No Montmorency tart cherry sleep RCT in adolescents, shift workers, perimenopausal women or people on sleep medication was found; no trial longer than 30 days was found for sleep; no adverse-event data beyond the abstracts were found (abstracts rarely report safety; no serious tart-cherry-specific adverse events were reported in any cited abstract, which is not the same as proving safety).

No meta-analysis with pooled effects exists; the 2025 systematic review (PMID 40964149) is qualitative, reports 3 of 7 studies with improved sleep indicators and calls the evidence limited and heterogeneous.
The official pubmedUrl check could not return HTTP 200 from curl (NCBI returns a 203 challenge page); PMIDs, titles, journals and years were instead verified via E-utilities esummary (HTTP 200).
